title: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
desc: Makes gains conditional on task, workflow, support and self-knowledge rather than access or usage volume.

kps.k: AI productivity gains depend on the task, user and workflow—not access or model capability alone.
kps.d: The cluster shifts the debate from whether AI improves knowledge work to when gains emerge, who captures them and whether they persist. Experimental studies document faster or better task completion, while training studies, organizational reports and theoretical models identify complementary requirements: interaction skills, appropriate delegation, verification and workflow integration. These accounts differ substantively: Noy and Zhang characterize professional-writing assistance mainly as substitution for effort, whereas Anand and Idan emphasize complementary human capabilities. Neither mechanism establishes autonomous professional competence or economy-wide gains.

qs.q: ChatGPT mostly substitutes for worker effort rather than complementing       worker skills, and restructures tasks towards idea-generation and editing and away from       rough-drafting.
qs.a: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2023

qs.q: These insights reframe AI adoption as a problem of capability design rather than tool procurement.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Several studies find substantial task-level gains, often concentrated among weaker or less-experienced performers.
kps.d: The November 2023 version of Generative AI at Work studies staggered deployment among 5,179 customer-support workers and reports 14% more issues resolved per hour on average, with 34% gains for novice and low-skilled workers and minimal gains for experienced, highly skilled workers. Noy and Zhang’s supplied March 2023 writing experiment reports a 0.8-standard-deviation reduction in completion time and a 0.4-standard-deviation quality increase. Workplace Copilot trials estimate 26.08% more weekly completed tasks among users, with a 10.3% standard error. Separately, an experiment with 1,174 adults closes about three-quarters of an education-based business-task performance gap. These outcomes measure different dimensions of performance and do not support a single pooled productivity estimate or a conclusion about wage equality.

qs.q: Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raises average productivity: time taken       decreases by 0.8 SDs and output quality rises by 0.4 SDs.
qs.a: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2023

kps.k: Equalization is conditional: open-ended decisions and learning tasks can instead favor stronger users.
kps.d: Anand and Idan’s student experiment reports approximately 17% higher mean performance alongside a 47% increase in novice standard deviation; AI Interaction Competence moderates gains more strongly than conventional academic markers. The IELTS coaching experiments find larger benefits for students with higher baseline proficiency, which the authors explain through their ability to absorb and apply feedback. In Kenya, randomized business-advice access yields no statistically resolved average effect, but estimated outcomes improve by just over 15% for initially stronger entrepreneurs and decline by about 8% for weaker ones. The authors attribute divergence to selecting and implementing advice. These findings qualify universal equalizer claims rather than directly contradicting gains on constrained tasks. Education, experience, baseline performance and AI interaction competence remain distinct measures.

qs.q: However, dispersion among novices increased by roughly 47% in standard deviation—more than doubling the variance.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

qs.q: First, AI coaching significantly improves student writing performance and independent practice intensity, yet these benefits are disproportionately greater for students with higher baseline proficiency.
qs.a: Does AI Equalize or Amplify? Evidence from Two Field Experiments in AI-powered Learning · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Training and structured support can improve outcomes, but more usage is not itself evidence of productive use.
kps.d: Training for Technology randomizes 164 Hong Kong law students across no access, access alone and access plus brief instruction. Trained students use AI more and score nearly one fine grade above the access-only group; access alone does not improve average performance, and its small negative score difference does not establish harm. Training expands adoption, but the design cannot sharply identify improved effectiveness among people who would use AI anyway. Anand and Idan find that conceptual scaffolding reduces novice dispersion without lowering mean performance, whereas extra study time adds no significant gain. IELTS information-design interventions improve learning without increasing total AI usage. These results support targeted instruction, not a universal training formula; legal-practice transfer and optimal training design remain unresolved.

qs.q: Compared to participants who only had access to an LLM, participants who received the intervention reported substantially higher rates of GenAI usage and achieved, on average, scores that were better by nearly one fine grade.
qs.a: Training for Technology: Adoption and Productive Use of Generative AI in Legal Analysis · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Notably, a scaffolding intervention (conceptual roadmaps and sequencing) reduced this dispersion by nearly 40% without lowering the mean, demonstrating that small process changes can stabilize outcomes.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Effective reliance requires recognizing both AI’s limitations and one’s own.
kps.d: The BCG experiments find faster, higher-quality work on tasks within GPT-4’s capabilities, but a 19-percentage-point correctness penalty on a selected task outside them. Recommendation quality improves even when the underlying answer is wrong, separating persuasive output from substantive correctness. The ABC’s experiment finds the largest gains among low-ability participants with accurate self-beliefs; holding ability fixed, a one-standard-deviation calibration difference corresponds to a 20% larger treatment effect. Lee and colleagues’ survey associates greater confidence in AI with less reported critical thinking and greater self-confidence with more. That survey measures perceptions, not causal cognitive decline. Together, these sources distinguish calibrated reliance from either blanket trust or blanket avoidance.

qs.q: For a task selected to be outside the frontier, however, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions compared to those without AI.
qs.a: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Assisted performance and independent skill formation can move in different directions.
kps.d: Shen and Tamkin’s programming experiments find impaired conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging without significant average efficiency gains. Conceptual questioning and explanation-seeking associate with stronger learning, but usage strategies were not separately randomized. Countervailing evidence includes persistent customer-support gains during AI outages and modest immediate unassisted carryover among lower-education participants in the business-task experiment. Neither establishes universal or durable learning. Aouad, Lykouris and Zhong model conditions under which reduced effort, unreliable assistance and unequal AI literacy reverse gains or polarize skills; these are conditional theoretical results. The Cognitive Commons framework extends the concern to replenishing professional expertise, while explicitly acknowledging that expertise remains healthy across most domains today.

qs.q: We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without                                                delivering significant efficiency gains on average.
qs.a: How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Using data on software outages—periods in which the AI software fails to provide any suggestions—we show that workers see productivity gains relative to their pre-AI baseline even when recommendations are unavailable.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

kps.k: AI can replace some collaborative functions without eliminating the value of human teams.
kps.d: The P&G experiment with 776 experienced professionals finds that AI-assisted individuals match unaided pairs and produce more balanced cross-functional proposals. AI-assisted pairs do not significantly outperform AI-assisted individuals on average, but more often produce top-decile proposals. One-day collaborations cannot establish effects on sustained coordination, rework or expertise development. Hoffmann and colleagues also report shifts toward coding and away from project-management activity among developers below the median on ability proxies; flatter hierarchies remain a possible implication. For agentic systems, the Codex source argues that delegation makes review processes and coordination more important, but its usage differences do not identify those factors’ separate causal contributions.

qs.q: Our findings reveal that AI significantly enhances performance: individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI, demonstrating that AI can effectively replicate certain benefits of human collaboration.
qs.a: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise · Academia · 2025

qs.q: For each of these measures, we find that individuals below the median (low ability) exhibit larger increases of coding activities and larger reductions in project management activities, as a percentage of all activities, than those above the median (high ability).
qs.a: Generative AI and the Nature of Work · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Individual gains may carry collective costs in rework, creative diversity and expertise transmission.
kps.d: The Workslop authors argue that indiscriminate AI mandates encourage unsuitable output and shift remediation onto colleagues; their supplied claims draw on research and advisory experience rather than a controlled estimate of organization-wide productivity loss. Creative-writing research reports higher average creativity but warns that broader adoption could make outputs more alike. Diverse AI Personas challenges inevitability, proposing that configurable partners and varied prompts can counter uniformity; the supplied excerpt provides no quantitative comparison of designs. The BCG study and Matt Beane’s DORA contribution likewise argue for protecting learning and judging success beyond output volume. The practical tension concerns which objective an organization prioritizes: speed, correctness, exceptional quality, diversity or future competence.

qs.q: Gen AI gives us a new technology with which to lean into the same old bad habits—but now with the added cost of creating more work for our colleagues and undermining collaboration, at scale.
qs.a: AI-Generated "Workslop" Is Destroying Productivity · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Despite the enhancement effect that GenAI had on average creativity, we also believe our study offers a cautionary note if GenAI were adopted more widely for creative tasks.
qs.a: Generative AI Enhances Individual Creativity but Reduces the Collective Diversity of Novel Content · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Adoption, time savings, financial returns and aggregate productivity require separate measurement.
kps.d: The Rapid Adoption study reports weekly workplace use by 23% of employed respondents in late 2024, but estimates AI use occupied only 1–5% of total work hours. Its approximately 1.1% potential productivity gain comes from self-reported savings and an aggregate-production model, not observed aggregate growth. The GenAI Divide claims 95% of organizations receive zero return, drawing on interviews, surveys and public implementations; this is a report-level claim, not a causal economy-wide estimate. The Professional Services Report separately finds that more than half of respondents’ organizations do not measure ROI—absence of measurement does not establish absence of return. Workflow bottlenecks, adoption differences and complementary investment offer explanations for incomplete translation from task gains to final output, but their magnitudes remain uncertain.

qs.q: Combining detailed data on the frequency and intensity of genAI usage, we estimate that between 1 and 5 percent of total work hours in the previous week were spent using genAI.
qs.a: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Despite $30–40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI, this report uncovers a surprising result in that 95% of organizations are getting zero return.
qs.a: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Narrower performance gaps do not establish better employment prospects or lower economic inequality.
kps.d: Customer-support and education-gap studies explicitly leave wages and aggregate labor demand unresolved. Seniority-Biased Technological Change interprets its 2023–2025 evidence as suggesting narrower entry routes, but acknowledges residual confounding and incomplete adoption measurement. The August 2026 Canaries revision explicitly labels its indicators descriptive rather than causal. Models of skill homogenization argue that task convergence can coexist with asset concentration, while diffusion studies suggest unequal access may widen disparities. These remain distinct mechanisms and evidence types. For legal employers and educators, the practical implication advanced across the cluster is to pair task-specific training and verification with protected learning opportunities, and measure final work quality, downstream effort and independent competence—not adoption alone. The supplied judicial and legal-review excerpts do not establish practice-wide productivity effects.

qs.q: Unfortunately, our data do not allow us to observe changes in wages, overall labor demand, or the skill composition of workers hired for the job.
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Accordingly, we do not interpret our estimates as direct predictions about wage effects or aggregate equilibrium inequality.
qs.a: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition that AI’s productivity distribution is conditional on task structure, user capabilities, workflow design and support rather than access or usage alone. They materially develop it through randomized field and workplace experiments, controlled learning studies, observational labour-market research and conditional theoretical models. Common explanations for uneven gains include whether tasks are constrained or open-ended; users’ ability to absorb, select, verify and implement AI output; calibrated self-knowledge; cognitive engagement; training and scaffolding; and organizational integration. Material internal variation concerns the direction and endpoint of effects. Constrained writing, customer-support, coding and some consulting tasks often favor weaker or less-experienced users, whereas learning and open-ended business decisions can favor stronger users or harm weaker ones. Some sources further separate immediate assisted output from independent skill formation, career ladders, enterprise returns and aggregate productivity. The evidence base also varies in strength: randomized experiments support several task-level causal claims, while long-run skill polarization, expertise depletion, employment effects and macroeconomic consequences remain modeled, descriptive or prospective. One excerpt on human-capital commoditization is too incomplete to determine its position. This synthesis describes only the curated sources supplied and should not be read as representing academia or researchers generally.

vlens.an: These selected legal-tech-vendor sources accept the proposition that AI gains are conditional on more than access, adoption or model capability, and collectively develop it in three material directions. The Codex source provides the strongest extension: for agentic AI, value depends on organizational redesign around delegation, verification, coordination and downstream workflow bottlenecks, so task-level gains may not become final-output gains. The DORA contribution adds an intertemporal dimension, arguing that organizations should protect interpersonal expertise transmission and measure skill development alongside immediate output; however, this is primarily prescriptive reasoning rather than empirical evidence. Google’s ATLAS adds labour-market caution: task exposure is not equivalent to end-to-end automation, and augmentation may increase returns to non-routine skills and potentially widen wage inequality rather than consistently equalize outcomes. Internal variation therefore concerns level of analysis and evidentiary status—not the core position: Codex focuses on organizational implementation and draws partly on reported studies; DORA emphasizes learning and future competence conceptually; ATLAS focuses on economy-wide exposure and distribution while explicitly treating wage effects as prospective and labour-market evidence as unsettled. Because this is a curated selection, these commonalities should not be read as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.
qs.a: The Shift to Agentic AI: Evidence from Codex · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the proposition that GenAI gains depend on task characteristics, workflow integration and complementary human capabilities rather than access or usage alone. The Professional Services Report approaches this principally at the organisational level: adoption and familiarity are insufficient without strategic alignment, ROI measurement, policy and training. The Future of Jobs Report approaches it at the skill and task level: substitution potential varies across activities, while human oversight and GenAI literacy remain important complements. Material variation lies in evidence and emphasis. The former relies on reported organisational readiness and communication gaps; the latter models current skill-substitution capacity rather than measuring realised productivity or its distribution among stronger and weaker users. Thus, these sources reinforce the cluster’s conditional account but do not directly establish which user groups gain most.

vlens.an: The OECD source supports the proposition that AI productivity gains are conditional on the worker, task and organizational setting rather than following uniformly from access. It reports measured gains concentrated among less-experienced customer-support workers, consistent with AI narrowing performance differences in a constrained workflow. At the same time, its survey evidence introduces material variation: university graduates and workers in professional or managerial occupations report greater improvements than less-educated, production or non-supervisory workers. This suggests that weaker or less-experienced users do not invariably benefit most, although those survey results concern perceived rather than independently measured performance. The OECD also cautions that evidence from narrowly scoped applications may not generalise across firms. As a single curated source from this professional voice, it supports contextual and heterogeneous gains but does not establish their prevalence across regulators, courts and professional bodies.

qs.q: The researchers find that the gains in productivity mostly accrue to the least experienced  workers, suggesting that the generative AI application infers and implicitly conveys the behavioural  patterns of the most productive customer support workers to those who are least skilled or experienced.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: worker productivity is consistent with emerging studies of adoption of generative AI applications in the workplace, although these applications tend to be quite specific in scope, and it is too soon to see how they generalise to a wider set of firms (see Box 4.2).

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI productivity gains are conditional rather than uniformly concentrated among weaker users, and materially develop it by identifying why outcomes vary. Across bounded writing, customer-support, creative and consulting tasks, several experiments find higher average performance and disproportionate gains for lower-ability or less-experienced participants. However, the sources consistently limit those findings to particular tasks, samples and workflows rather than treating AI as a universal equalizer. The most important extensions are that accurate self-assessment affects whether low-ability users capture gains; tasks outside the model’s capability frontier can produce lower correctness despite more persuasive output; individual creativity gains may reduce aggregate diversity; and task-level cost savings do not establish aggregate productivity, worker welfare or equitable distribution. Internal variation concerns mechanism and scope: writing assistance is characterized mainly as substituting for effort, while other accounts emphasize human–AI complementarity, calibration, verification and workflow design. Survey evidence reports perceived gains that vary by occupation and education, whereas randomized studies measure task performance directly. Macroeconomic analysis further warns against inferring economy-wide or distributional outcomes from proof-of-concept experiments. These are complementary qualifications and extensions, not substantive opposition to the cluster proposition; the curated sources should not be read as representing all research from the period.

qs.q: Second, we find that participants with high calibration and low ability gain the most from working with AI.
qs.a: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration · Academia · 2024

qs.q: For a task selected to be outside the frontier, however, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions compared to those without AI.
qs.a: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality · Academia · 2023

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that GenAI gains are conditional on task, user, workflow, support and calibrated reliance rather than access or usage volume alone. They materially extend it from individual task performance to adoption at organizational scale. Common reasons include the gap between tool uptake and strategic integration; limited ROI measurement and work-hour penetration; the need for training, human oversight, verification, contextual learning and workflow redesign; and the possibility that individual efficiency gains create downstream rework, weakened collaboration, reduced creative diversity or impaired expertise transmission. Material variation concerns where benefits and costs arise. Workplace studies report larger gains or task-allocation shifts among weaker or less-experienced workers, while other sources do not measure distribution by ability and instead focus on organizational readiness. The P&G experiment finds that AI-assisted individuals can replace some collaborative functions on average but that AI-assisted teams retain an advantage for exceptional outputs. Labour-market sources distinguish productivity equalization from employment outcomes, cautiously suggesting narrower entry-level career ladders while acknowledging confounding, incomplete adoption measurement and short observation periods. Evidence quality also varies: randomized and workplace studies provide bounded empirical findings, whereas surveys, organizational reports and design arguments mainly provide associations, implementation claims or prescriptions. No supplied source clearly rejects the proposition, but the curated set should not be treated as representative of all 2025 views.

qs.q: At the same time, however, initial adoption does not necessarily equal true integration into organizations’ strategy at large.
qs.a: 2025 Generative AI in Professional Services Report · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Most fail due to brittle workflows, lack of contextual learning, and misalignment with day-to-day operations.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develop it with new field experiments, controlled studies, organizational evidence and conditional models. Their common explanation is complementarity: outcomes depend on task structure, baseline knowledge, AI-interaction competence, judgment, cognitive engagement, training, verification and workflow integration—not access, usage volume or model capability alone. Material variation concerns the direction and level of the effect. Fixed, constrained execution tasks can disproportionately lift less-educated or less-experienced users, while open-ended business decisions and skill-acquisition tasks can favor stronger users or produce losses among weaker ones. Training and scaffolding can improve or stabilize outcomes, but added exposure alone may not. Workplace coding trials establish task-level output gains, whereas agentic-AI analyses emphasize downstream bottlenecks and organizational redesign. Theoretical work and the Cognitive Commons account extend the concern to skill decay, polarization and expertise regeneration, but these are conditional mechanisms or prospective risks rather than demonstrated economy-wide effects. Diffusion, judicial and labour-market sources further caution that adoption, exposure and benchmark capability do not establish final-output, employment, wage or aggregate-productivity effects.
